newsitem.title: INDIA: India shares end lower in nervous trade.
newsitem.headline: India shares end lower in nervous trade.

text.p: Indian stocks ended with small losses on Thursday as operators turned nervous ahead of expected market-policy initiatives, dealers said.
"Trading was very volatile. People who were hopeful about government announcements are suddenly turning a little less upbeat," said Hiren Ved, an equities analyst at Prime Securities.
The benchmark 30-share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) closed 15.92 points, or 0.45 percent, down to end at 3,510.05. Volumes on the BSE totalled 76.36 billion rupees.
"There was a lack of direction for market players...they didn't know what to do," Prime's Ved said.

Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda had on Monday promised the government would announce new economic measures before he left on Friday for a summit meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland.

India's market regulator the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) said late on Thursday it had approved a new takeover code for companies and a stock lending scheme. It also permitted foreign institutions to take up government debt.
Under the stock lending scheme lenders will deposit securities with an approved intermediary, which must have a minimum net worth of 500 million rupees for a specified period.
"It's a move in the right direction. The stock lending will bring more liquidity in the markets," said Sanjay Agarwal, chief executive at Lloyds Securities.
Late on Thursday Finance Minister P. Chidambaram released a list of decisions the government took this month to spur the economy. He said they amounted to a package of economic reforms.
"Taken together, I believe, they constitute a cohesive package of decisions which will impart greater thrust to economic reforms," Chidambaram said in a statement.
The list, which includes the decisions to allow foreign portfolio investment in debt and government gilts, was announced before Deve Gowda's visit, with Chidambaram, to Davos.
The Finance Minister is scheduled to present the 1997/98 (April-March) budget to parliament on February 28.
High expectations of the market-friendly initiatives promised by Deve Gowda have driven up Indian stocks by nearly 24 percent in less than a month.
"Typically, markets tend to rise only if expectations are more than met. It is the same here," said Prashant Purker, head of sales at Peregrine Capital.
"People did expect a lot, so I see a letdown in market sentiments which might be reflected in lower prices on Friday," Lloyds' Agarwal said.
Traders had hoped for tax breaks on company dividends, the easing of carry-forward rules for stock markets and a buy-back of shares, among other things.
Most players expect share prices to stay volatile in a market that they say is largely sentiment-driven.
"This (Thursday) is not a great day for capital markets. I see a major correction ahead," said Vijay Pandya, chief dealer at Classic Share & Stock Brokers.
